newsitem.title: USA: Indiana gov and lawmakers to meet on arena impasse.
newsitem.headline: Indiana gov and lawmakers to meet on arena impasse.

text.p: Indiana Gov. Frank O'Bannon and legislative leaders are scheduled to meet Tuesday afternoon to try to break an impasse that has delayed financing for a partly bond-financed new Indiana Pacers basketball arena and Indianapolis convention center expansion.

O'Bannon will urge the leaders to resolve their differences and pass bills addressing the arena, convention center, an inheritance tax cut and workers compensation coverage, spokesman Steve Campbell said.
Lawmakers approved a $17.5 billion biennium budget during a special session earlier this month, but failed to address the two major capital projects following a dispute over workers compensation.
House Democrats had sought to include an increase in workers compensation with the arena and convention center legislation, but House Republicans refused to consider the amendment.
The Indiana House has 50 Republicans and 50 Democrats.

House Republican Leader Paul Mannweiler, R-Indianapolis, has said repeatedly that he believes their is a less than 50 percent chance that lawmakers will break their stalemate, chief legal counsel Roger Schmelzer said Tuesday.
"The line in the sand is pretty bright," Schmelzer said. "I don't think the governor is going to be able to resolve it."
A spokesman for House Speaker John Gregg, D-Sandborn, said representatives had hoped to hold a session Tuesday, but were trying to reach a compromise for a planned session on Wednesday.
"Both sides are pretty adamant about what they want to bring to the table," Judson Kring said.

Financing for the estimated $175 million basketball arena would include $50 million of bonds backed in part by sales and income taxes derived from a new professional sports development district in downtown Indianapolis that needs legislative approval.

The convention center financing includes $40 million of bonds backed partly by increases in the hotel/motel tax, rental car tax and a broader application of the ticket tax. All three proposals need legislative approval and support of the Indianapolis City Council.
